title: The Philippine Immigration Detention Center: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with prices posted on the wall: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every one of them bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who jack up prices on the spot — is the part that's actually worth your time.
who: Founders and going-global operators interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the corruption machinery linking gray-market industries to the immigration bureau.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The immigration bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, an immigration officer pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the word came back: hand over 1.5 million pesos, roughly 160,000 to 170,000 RMB, and you can walk out immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 or 13 people arrested in the same batch, not one agreed to pay. Everyone thought there was no way this could still be happening in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal channels. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General City police station to the detention center at the Bureau of Immigration headquarters in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed this was standard procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and could not get the phone back, until he kept pressuring the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and only then was it returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but then transferred back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili said it wasn't about the amount; it was that the phone had been tampered with while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese doing gray-market scams in Manila go through this same shakedown after being arrested, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones are full of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the immigration bureau promised were just another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, the immigration bureau would work on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau were excellent — air conditioning, plenty of freedom, you can work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying: there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout — it was just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the headquarters detention center at past three in the morning. What he saw after getting out of the vehicle was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, and all around it iron cages like dog kennels, with long communal sleeping platforms inside, hundreds of people. At past three in the morning many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the iron cages staring at the newcomers. Feili said the few foreigners said nothing for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: the immigration bureau had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the immigration bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities had all been newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The cheapest communal-platform bed was 10,000 pesos a month, roughly 1,100 to 1,200 RMB. Wealthy pang zong and gambling bosses could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — in reality the bed was the same, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a styrofoam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan pulling the cold air into the bed. That's where the immigration bureau's claim that "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, that he'd come here to serve time — how could he be expected to pay on top of that. The gang boss said in a threatening tone: you're already in here and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes everything for Chinese inmates — food, clothing, daily life — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the off-season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them in gambling and gray industries. The Chinese gang's employees drew wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 pesos — very low pay, but many people couldn't get out precisely because they had no money for a lawyer, so they could only work to earn.

points.h: A young man from Yunnan was held over a year; his family thought he'd died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom scams. With poor performance he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own plane ticket, and you're gone — but the immigration bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he'd died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterward the immigration bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The Chinese man Feili talked with most was from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the immigration bureau together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first shakedown was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet — because there are no cameras in toilets — and taking everything valuable off them. The second was the immigration bureau negotiating ransoms with the company boss, with different quotes per person — 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos — depending on the mood of whoever was in charge. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was hit with a false illegal-possession-of-a-firearm charge by a corrupt cop, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raises his price on the spot when he sees you're Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, to get it done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, 41 days total including Cebu. The Lithuanian who'd introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.

quotes.text: You give him 1.5 million pesos now, you can walk out immediately, you'll have no problem at all.
But this isn't about the amount of money. When the phone wasn't in my hands, money was transferred out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and his ordinary people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are by nature very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — the kind of bureaucratic system that drinks blood, human blood.
